DOMESTIC ABUSE AWARENESS TRAINING FOR ELECTED MEMBERS & STAFF 
Jackie Carroll and Ciara Tyrrell of COPE Galway Domestic Abuse Service were delighted to be 
invited to deliver Domestic Abuse Awareness Training to Staff and Councillors of Galway 
County Council on Tuesday 12th of February. The training took place in the county chambers 
and participants explored the dynamics of abusive relationships, the many barriers that 
women face when attempting to leave and the effects that the abuse has on children. The 
training also explored how to recognise and respond and where to refer victim/survivors for 
support. With 1 in 3 women in Ireland experiencing domestic abuse it is important that we 
take a collaborate approach to holding perpetrators of abuse accountable and work towards 
removing the barriers that force women and children to leave home in the current housing 
crisis climate.  
Feedback from the training was positive and participants also had the opportunity to learn 
about the wide range of supports that COPE Galway Domestic Abuse Service provides. This 
includes Modh Eile, a 24-hour refuge for women and their children needing a place of 
safety. A free and confidential Outreach Service that provides supports for women and 
children throughout Galway City and County and Solas Óg a support service and education 
programme for children and young people up to the age of 25.  
If you or anyone you know are experiencing abuse, please contact our 24hour helpline no 
091 565985 for support and information.

LOCAL ENHANCEMENT PROGRAMME 2026  
Galway County Council has received funding of €213,600 from the Department of Rural and 
Community Development and the Gaeltacht under the Local Enhancement Programme 
2026.  This fund will provide capital funding to support community groups across Ireland.

10 
 
The funding will support groups, particularly in disadvantaged areas to carry out necessary 
repairs and improvements to their facilities, purchase equipment such as tables and chairs, 
tools and signage, laptops and printers, training equipment, and improving energy efficiency 
of community facilities to reduce ongoing costs.  
 
This year’s programme places particular focus on designated Community Support Centres 
following Storm Eowyn in January 2025, when many rural areas of Galway were left without 
electricity for extended periods. Groups are invited to apply for funding to help purchase a 
generator, as well as for the supply and installation of a changeover switch, enabling the use 
of a county-owned mobile generator to maintain essential services during future 
disruptions. 
 
In line with previous years, the LCDC will endeavour to allocate 30% of this fund towards 
small grants of €1,000 or less to maximise its benefit to small grassroots groups.  
This funding is now open for applications with a closing date of Friday 27th February 2026. 
Funding recommendations of the LCDC will be submitted to the Department of Rural and 
Community Development and the Gaeltacht by 22nd April 2026, for funding announcements 
by the Minister for Rural & Community Development & Gaeltacht in May 2026. All capital 
projects will be required to be completed and grants drawn down by the end of October 
2026.

THE WOMEN’S HEALTH PROGRAM 
Healthy County Galway is continuing to deliver its women’s health programme in 2026, 
building on strong participation and positive outcomes. Looking ahead to 2026, the 
programme has been redesigned to offer a more tailored and practical model, featuring a 
series of live-streamed talks and demonstrations broadcast simultaneously to a network of 
venues across Galway County and the offshore islands. The newly revised format consists of 
three weekly morning workshops and has been shaped by participant feedback. This 
approach is intended to keep the programme engaging and relevant to the needs of women 
in local communities. 
Greater emphasis is being placed on practical demonstrations 
and actionable advice to support women in perimenopause, 
menopause or post menopause to adopt healthier daily habits 
and sustaining these changes over time. Evaluation will also be 
strengthened, with an increased focus on returning participants, 
identifying lifestyle improvements and gathering insights into 
areas where additional support may be beneficial. This approach 
ensures the programme continues to evolve but remains rooted 
in its goal to empower women to take an active role in their own 
health and wellbeing.

OUTDOOR RECREATION  
Galway County Council has established a new committee to coordinate the delivery of 
sustainable outdoor trails, parks and water-based infrastructure across County Galway, 
including trails, parks and water-based infrastructure. 
  
Working under the National Outdoor Recreation Strategy 2023–2027, the Galway County 
Outdoor Recreation Committee brings together local government, community and voluntary 
organisations and key state agencies to support a coordinated, countywide approach to 
outdoor recreation. 
  
The committee held its first meeting on Thursday, 5 February, in the Council Chamber at Áras 
an Chontae, where members agreed its remit, set initial priorities for 2026 and began work 
on shared actions to expand outdoor recreation opportunities across the county. 
 
A separate Galway Outdoor Recreation Project Team has also been established to support the 
Committee. It met for the first time on 21 January and will lead the preparation of the Galway 
County Outdoor Recreation Strategy 2026-2030, which has been approved for funding by the 
Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht. The five-year plan will 
guide investment and development across the sector.

PROJECT: RURAL PROOFING COOP4RURALGOV 
 
Rural Proofing, Cooperation for better 
governance with a rural approach, will foster 
inter-regional cooperation and exchange 
between 7 public and private organisations 
from Spain, Estonia, Ireland and Bulgaria to 
improve their governance' capacities for co-

STUDY VISIT ON RURAL PROOFING GOOD PRACTICES IN FINLAND UNDER THE 
COOP4RURALGOV PROJECT 
 13-14 January 2026 
   Helsinki, Finland 
On the 13th and 14th of January, 2026, a Study visit within the frame of the Coop4RURALGov 
project “Rural Proofing. Cooperation for better sparsely populated rural, coastal and

15 
 
mountain focused governance” took place in Helsinki, Finland. The visit brought together 
project partners and experts from Spain, Bulgaria, Estonia, and Ireland to learn from 
Finland’s long-standing experience in integrating rural perspectives into public policy and 
governance. 
Finland was selected as a host country due to its well-established Rural Proofing system. 
With the majority of its territory classified as rural, Finland provides a relevant and proven 
reference model for evidence-based, 
participatory and territorially 
sensitive governance. 
ATTENDING: BERNIE DONNELLAN, 
COMMUNITY, RURAL TOURISM AND 
INTEGRATION DEPARTMENT. 
SINÉAD QUINN, RURAL STRATEGY 
UNIT. DEPARTMENT OF RURAL AND 
COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT AND 
THE GAELTACHT 
 
The main objective of the visit was to enable partners 
to directly explore the Finnish Rural Proofing 
ecosystem, understand its governance structures and 
assessment tools, and identify transferable practices 
for implementation in their own regions. 
 
Finland is one of the most rural countries in the EU, with 
95% of its land area classified as rural and roughly a third 
of the population living in rural areas. Rural policy and 
rural development are crucially important for Finnish 
Government so in 2007, Finland began working on a Rural 
Proofing strategy based on previous international experiences. Since then, the country has 
continued to develop its “Rural Guarantee”.  
The first day focused on Finland’s policy ecosystem 
for Rural Proofing and its integration into national 
governance. Representatives from the Ministry of 
Agriculture and Forestry presented the evolution of 
Rural Proofing as part of the National Rural Policy 
Programme, highlighting inter-ministerial 
coordination and cooperation with local authorities. 
Participants were introduced to the systematic integration of rural impact assessment in 
national decision-making processes, supported by data-driven evaluations and stakeholder 
participation. A practical example demonstrated how Rural Proofing is embedded in digital

16 
 
preliminary impact assessment tools, illustrating how rural considerations are incorporated 
into modern governance instruments. 
During the second working day, concrete 
applications of Rural Proofing in legislative and 
strategic processes were showcased. Participants 
were also introduced to a newly developed Rural 
Transport Impact Assessment tool, designed to 
reveal hidden mobility and accessibility impacts 
of public decisions on rural areas. The day 
concluded with insights into Rural Proofing implementation at a municipal level, highlighting 
opportunities and practical constraints faced by 
local authorities. 
The study visit provided valuable insights and 
practical knowledge to support the transfer of 
effective Rural Proofing methodologies to 
partner regions, contributing to more inclusive 
and territorially balanced governance. 
Rural Proofing is not a policy, it is designed to be a “process” that enables decision makers 
to “think rural” when designing policy interventions in order to prevent negative outcomes 
or, even better, trigger positive outcomes in rural areas. Further information: www.gov.ie  
Rural proofing is an approach that helps ensure that the development of key government 
policies considers and takes account of rural perspectives and priorities. Following research, 
which considered international experience, and a pilot to apply rural proofing concepts to 
policy development, the Department of Rural and Community Development has developed 
a Guide to Rural Proofing for Policy Makers to help them to think about the rural context 
when developing policies

2026 CREATIVE IRELAND OPEN CALL 
This year’s Creative Ireland Open Call ran from the 16th of December to the 23rd of January. 
During that time two online information sessions were held, both of which were well 
attended. The decision was made this year to lower the maximum grant amount from 
€8,000 to €6,000 and to also run a concurrent Open Call for Creativity Newcomers. The 
purpose of this was to encourage groups who have not previously engaged with the 
Creative Ireland programme to take on a creative project. The maximum grant amount for 
Newcomers was set at €2,500. In total 56 completed applications were received via 
Submit.com. Of those submitted, 50 were deemed eligible and approved for shortlisting. Of 
those 50, 32 fell into the Newcomer category. The 50 shortlisted applications went to the 
panel for assessment with a total of 25 groups receiving funding, 14 of which were 
Newcomers. This was an incredibly high success rate as previous years have seen less than 
20% of applicants receive offers of funding. This dramatic increase was largely due to the 
smaller grant amounts as the total amount of available funding did not change from last 
year. The total amount of funding offered for the 2026 Creative Ireland Open Call is 
€70,392. The Creativity Newcomers programme has seen engagement from Active 
Retirement Groups, Mens Sheds, and 
Community Garden Projects. All in all it is 
shaping up to be a very busy but 
extremely rewarding and engaging year 
in Galway County Council’s Creative 
Ireland programme.

INTRODUCTION 
This report provides an expanded analysis of Tenancy & Estate Management (TEM) activity 
during 2025, highlighting complaint trends, estate‑based intervention outcomes, 
enforcement activity, and the Council’s statutory duty‑of‑care responsibilities. It also 
outlines the planned expansion of the “Boots on the Ground” model for 2026. 
COMPLAINT TRENDS AND SERVICE DEMAND 
The year 2025 saw a significant increase in tenancy‑related complaints, driven by higher 
tenant engagement, visibility of staff in estates, and improved reporting channels. 
COMPLAINTS RECEIVED, CLOSED AND OPEN YEAR‑END 
 
• Complaints received rose from 118 in 2024 to 188 in 2025—a 59% increase. 
• Complaints closed increased to 131, but the overall closure rate fell from 92.4% to 
69.7% due to the higher volume of cases. 
• Open cases at year‑end increased sharply from 9 to 57, representing a six‑fold rise. 
INTERPRETATION OF TRENDS 
The scale of the increase reflects a combination of factors: 
• Greater visibility of TEM officers during estate visits encouraged more tenants to 
report issues directly. 
• Early‑stage issues previously unreported were identified through proactive checks. 
• Increased public awareness of reporting pathways contributed to higher demand. 
This shift indicates a more engaged tenant base but also highlights increasing operational 
pressure on case resolution capacity. 
ESTATE VISITS AND PROACTIVE ENGAGEMENT 
In 2025, the TEM team conducted 19 structured estate visits, forming a cornerstone of the 
Council’s proactive estate‑management strategy. 
KEY OPERATIONAL OUTCOMES 
 
• Household Composition Regulation: Officers corrected multiple cases of unapproved 
household changes, improving the accuracy of tenancy records. 
• Restricted Dog Breed Compliance: Non‑compliant tenants were identified, advised 
and monitored to bring them into conformity with legislation.

47 
 
• Waste Management Enforcement: Officers negotiated new waste arrangements, 
significantly reducing refuse‑related issues. 
• Resident Participation: Support was provided to new or emerging Residents’ 
Associations, strengthening local community structures.  
ENHANCED BENEFITS OBSERVED 
The visits also yielded broader community and compliance benefits: 
• Strengthened trust between tenants and Council staff. 
• Earlier identification of risks such as overcrowding or property neglect. 
• Improved estate cleanliness and safety through direct action. 
• Greater tenant awareness of responsibilities and reduced incidence of repeat 
breaches. 
These benefits demonstrate the value of sustained on‑site presence and early intervention. 
ENFORCEMENT ACTIVITY AND LEGAL OUTCOMES 
Enforcement remains a critical tool for addressing serious tenancy breaches and 
safeguarding communities. 
ENFORCEMENT FIGURES FOR 2025 
• 100% court success rate across all cases progressed. 
• 4 possession orders secured:  
o 2 in Ballinasloe 
o 1 in Tuam 
o 1 in Kinvara 
• 1 exclusion order obtained in Oranmore.  
IMPORTANCE OF ENFORCEMENT 
Successful legal action: 
• Sends a clear message that tenancy conditions will be upheld. 
• Protects compliant tenants from anti‑social behaviour and intimidation. 
• Reinforces the Council’s commitment to safe and peaceful communities. 
• Supports officers by ensuring investigative work leads to enforceable outcomes. 
DUTY OF CARE AND INTEGRATED APPROACH 
The Council’s legal and ethical duty to ensure tenants experience peaceful enjoyment, 
safety, and a harassment‑free environment is central to the structure of TEM operations. 
The integration of:

48 
 
• Complaint handling, 
• Estate visits, and 
• Legal enforcement 
creates a cohesive pathway from early detection to resolution. This coordinated model 
ensures issues are addressed proportionately, promptly, and in a manner that protects 
community wellbeing. 
OUTLOOK FOR 2026: EXPANSION OF “BOOTS ON THE GROUND” 
Building on the successes of 2025, the Council plans to significantly increase the scope and 
frequency of estate visits in 2026. 
PLANNED ENHANCEMENTS 
• Greater presence in new housing developments, where early engagement is most 
impactful. 
• More structured, frequent visits to ensure early identification of emerging issues. 
• Focus on supporting the growth of resident‑led groups, embedding positive estate 
culture from the outset. 
EXPECTED BENEFITS 
• Improved compliance and reduced long‑term casework. 
• Stronger tenant–Council relationships. 
• More stable and safer estates. 
• Reduced escalation to enforcement by addressing problems at source. 
CONCLUSION 
The 2025 operational year was characterised by substantial increases in tenant 
engagement and complaint volumes, enhanced by the proactive presence of officers in 
estates. Despite the increased workload, the Council achieved important compliance 
outcomes, improved tenant relationships, and maintained a robust enforcement record. 
The planned expansion of on‑site engagement in 2026 positions the Council to further 
strengthen estate management, support tenants, and uphold its duty to protect safe and 
peaceful communities
